subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Where was the painkiller aspirin originally derived from?
questions.explain: Aspirin originates from a chemical found in willow bark; many drugs originally came from plants.

questions.q: Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) affects which type of organism?
questions.explain: TMV is a plant pathogen that causes a mosaic pattern of discolouration on leaves, reducing photosynthesis.

questions.q: What is the main role of stomach acid in defending against disease?
options: It traps dust in the airways
It kills pathogens in swallowed food and mucus
questions.explain: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills most pathogens that are swallowed.

questions.q: Why is a variegated (green and white) leaf useful in a starch test experiment?
options: The white parts lack chlorophyll, so only green areas should make starch
questions.explain: Only the green parts have chlorophyll, so starch should form there, showing chlorophyll is needed.

questions.q: What is herd immunity?
options: When antibiotics are given to a whole population
When animals become immune to human diseases
When farm herds are vaccinated together
When enough people are vaccinated that a disease cannot spread easily, protecting the unvaccinated too
questions.explain: If a large proportion of a population is immune, pathogens struggle to spread, so even unvaccinated people are protected.

questions.q: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria such as MRSA are a problem because:
options: They are killed instantly by all antibiotics
They reproduce too slowly to spread
Existing antibiotics no longer kill them, so infections are hard to treat
questions.explain: Resistant bacteria survive treatment, making infections difficult to cure and able to spread between people.

questions.q: Increasing carbon dioxide concentration speeds up photosynthesis only until...
options: another factor such as light or temperature becomes limiting
questions.explain: CO2 increases the rate until another factor becomes limiting, then the rate levels off.

questions.q: At low light intensity, what is most likely limiting photosynthesis?
questions.explain: When light is in short supply it limits the rate, so increasing light increases photosynthesis.

questions.q: Glucose made in photosynthesis can be converted to which insoluble storage molecule?
questions.explain: Glucose is stored as insoluble starch, which does not affect the cell's water balance.

questions.q: During which stage are new drugs first tested for toxicity on cells, tissues and live animals?
questions.explain: Preclinical testing uses cells, tissues and animals before any human trials begin.

questions.q: Why are the upper palisade cells, rather than the lower spongy cells, packed with the most chloroplasts?
options: They are nearer the light at the top of the leaf
questions.explain: Palisade cells are at the top of the leaf where light is strongest, so they hold the most chloroplasts.

questions.q: Why can viruses NOT be treated with antibiotics?
options: Viruses are too large for antibiotics to reach
Viruses reproduce inside the body's own cells, where antibiotics cannot easily target them
Viruses are killed only by stomach acid
questions.explain: Viruses live and reproduce inside host cells, so antibiotics (which target bacterial processes) cannot kill them.

questions.q: Why does the rate of photosynthesis fall at very high temperatures?
questions.explain: High temperatures denature the enzymes needed for photosynthesis, so the rate falls.

questions.q: Light energy in photosynthesis is converted into which form of energy stored in glucose?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose.

questions.q: Painkillers such as paracetamol are useful but do NOT:
options: Kill the pathogen causing the illness
Make a patient feel more comfortable
questions.explain: Painkillers treat the symptoms of an illness but do not kill the pathogen, unlike antibiotics which kill bacteria.

questions.q: Which of these is a limiting factor for photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature can all limit the rate of photosynthesis.

questions.q: Why do palisade cells near the top of a leaf contain many chloroplasts?
options: To absorb maximum light for photosynthesis
questions.explain: Palisade mesophyll cells are packed with chloroplasts to capture as much light as possible.

questions.q: Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted disease caused by a bacterium. How can its spread be controlled?
questions.explain: Gonorrhoea is treated with antibiotics, and barrier methods such as condoms reduce its spread.

questions.q: Which disease is caused by a protist spread by mosquitoes?
questions.explain: Malaria is caused by a protist, with mosquitoes acting as vectors that transfer it between people.

questions.q: Whose work is most associated with the theory of evolution by natural selection?
questions.explain: Charles Darwin proposed evolution by natural selection in 'On the Origin of Species'.

questions.q: Cilia and mucus in the trachea and bronchi help defend the body by:
options: Trapping pathogens and wafting them away from the lungs
questions.explain: Mucus traps pathogens and tiny cilia sweep the mucus up away from the lungs, a non-specific defence.

questions.q: In which organelle does photosynthesis take place?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis occurs in the chloroplasts, which contain chlorophyll.
